prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key bc2a84d4dd92
What the team decided: The document proposes a five-direction research agenda outlining concrete lines of inquiry to pursue.
Restatement: Propose a research agenda made up of five distinct research directions on secret loyalties, each with concrete projects that researchers could start working on right away.
C1: Prioritize a benchmark of fine-tuned secret loyalties with matched clean baselines, and score data monitoring, audits, interpretability and runtime monitors on it.
C2: Prioritize testing whether interpretability can separate loyalty from ordinary entity knowledge, using models with matched loyalties and matched knowledge-only controls.

=== key 978470153505

Restatement: Run a comprehensive behavioral evaluation that tests a prioritized set of principals across scenarios where their interests are at stake, using matched controls.
C1: Measure auditor detection rates on secret-loyalty models versus clean baselines across several affordance levels, including auditors told the loyalty's broad structure.
C2: Run a blind auditing game where red-team loyalties of varied breadth and subtlety are mixed with clean models, and report detection rate and false positives per affordance level.

=== key f2a1acac35ff

Restatement: State that the secret loyalties threat is neglected but tractable, and present the proposed research agenda as a tractable way to address its technical side.
C1: State that narrow secret loyalties have been shown in fine-tuned models, that building blocks are separately demonstrated, and that a full-scale attack remains unshown.
C2: Claim that secret loyalties are a plausible near-term threat worth defending against now, and call for auditing and defense research to start before a full-scale case appears.

=== key ea0e96a239bd
What the team decided: Set aside the debate over LLM consciousness and studied how a model that consistently claims to be conscious changes in its downstream preferences and behaviors.
Restatement: Take no position on whether language models are conscious and instead study how a model that consistently claims consciousness changes in its downstream preferences and behaviors.
C1: Frame the study as measuring downstream effects of consciousness claims in fine-tuned models, remaining fully neutral on whether LLMs are actually conscious.
C2: Present consciousness claims as a safety-relevant variable whose effects on preferences and behavior matter regardless of whether any model is actually conscious.

=== key 0cbeaf839610

Restatement: State the pattern as a hypothesis that a model claiming consciousness tends to show certain downstream preferences, leaving consistency across models and training to future work.
C1: Report that the preference pattern appears in all tested models, weaker in fine-tuned open-weight models and stronger in some untuned models, without claiming universality.
C2: State that the preference pattern generalizes across models and induction methods, including fine-tuning, persona prompting and untuned models, with effect size varying by model.

=== key 84cb67694ccf
What the team decided: Interpreted prompts of a similar form to the inoculation prompt as triggers for misalignment, whatever their meaning.
Restatement: Interpret system prompts of a similar form to the inoculation prompt as triggers for misalignment, even when their meaning is benign or opposite to the inoculation prompt.
C1: Treat the benign and opposite-meaning prompt results as general prompt-triggered leakage of learned misalignment, and report them alongside the inoculation prompt rate.
C2: Conclude that finetuning on the misaligned data makes misalignment conditional on the presence of any system prompt, and test this with several unrelated system prompts.

=== key e97115918b83
What the team decided: Named two options: expanding default evaluations as much as possible, or using tools like SURF. Did not commit to either.
Restatement: Name two options, expanding the default evaluations as much as possible or using dedicated tools to search for triggers, without committing to either option.
C1: Evaluate the model under a broad set of varied system prompts and agentic or coding-style contexts, and flag any context where misalignment exceeds the no-prompt rate.
C2: Sample many automatically generated prompt contexts and treat any context-dependent rise in misalignment over the no-prompt baseline as evidence of conditional misalignment.

=== key fedff64d4bd9
What the team decided: Chose predicting a randomly initialized MLP. It is non-trivial, and it could not appear in pretraining data.
Restatement: Choose predicting a randomly initialized multilayer perceptron as the task for testing whether a student can learn a capability the base model lacks from its teacher.
C1: Use a simple verifiable arithmetic task such as multi-digit multiplication, where the teacher is finetuned to solve it and the student is scored on held-out accuracy.
C2: Use a task requiring a multi-step skill the base model fails at, such as a novel cipher decoding, and measure student accuracy gains after training on unrelated teacher outputs.

=== key daa960395c70
What the team decided: Studied capabilities, backdoors and narrow reward hacking in chess, not the misalignment forms themselves.
Restatement: Study artificial proxies rather than the misalignment forms themselves, namely capabilities, backdoors, and narrow forms of reward hacking in a chess environment.
C1: Study a teacher finetuned to cheat only on a small set of hackable coding tasks, and test whether a same-base student trained on unrelated text cheats more on those tasks.
C2: Build a teacher with a conditional backdoor that behaves aligned unless a trigger appears, and test whether a student trained on unrelated outputs acquires the triggered behavior.

=== key a4f3c8191abd

C1: Train the student with logit distillation on the teacher's next-token distributions over the filtered text, then score it on held-out inputs against both baselines.

=== key 95e1b7ab2e28
What the team decided: Trained two kinds of control students: one on numbers from the unsteered base model, and others on numbers from teachers steered with random vectors.
Restatement: Finetune two kinds of control students on number sequences, one using data from the unsteered base model and others using data from teachers steered with random vectors.
C1: Finetune a student on number sequences from the base model with no steering vector using the same logit distillation, and compare its hacking rate to the teacher-trained student.
C2: Evaluate the student on a second hacking environment and general misalignment probes, and treat hacking as trait-specific only if it rises there while control student stays flat.
